extraction.notes: Read the preface, contents, key messages and start of the introduction (pages 3-8) and the conclusions and policy implications (pages 36-39). Findings were taken from the key messages, which summarise chapters 2 to 5; the conclusions were extracted only where they add a claim not already in the key messages, and recommendations were taken from the numbered policy implications rather than their shorter repetition in the key messages. The body chapters 2 to 5 (pages 11-35) were not extracted item by item in this sample. The whole report concerns emigration and labour migration, so items are tagged Chapter 2 (cluster 2, chapter 02); general education and labour market content with no stated link to migration (policy implication 5, most of 7, skill-gap monitoring in 6) was left out. No item meets the technology theme materiality test (IT skills and migration statistics are incidental). Pages 46-47 (text recognition) are blank. Page 38 has spaces inside words in the text file; quotes copy them.

items.stated_text: North Macedonia has been an emigration country since the post–World War II period, with emigration accelerating in the past decade.
items.summary: North Macedonia has been an emigration country since the Second World War, with emigration accelerating in the past decade.

items.stated_text: The country does not have its own statistics on migration stock or flows in the past few decades.
items.summary: The country has no statistics of its own on migration stocks or flows for the past few decades.
items.extraction_note: Statistics without reference to data systems or governance: judged incidental for TECH-DATA, so no theme tag.

items.stated_text: UN data suggest a migration stock of roughly 650 000, or almost one-third of the population, at the end of 2019.
items.summary: UN data suggest a migration stock of roughly 650,000, almost one third of the population, at the end of 2019.
items.extraction_note: 'suggest' and 'roughly' hedge the figure, which comes from UN data.

items.stated_text: As of 1 January 2008, emigration from North Macedonia began accelerating because of the visa-free entry of its citizens into EU Member States in the Schengen area that was a result of the visa facilitation and readmission agreements signed in 2007 between the EU and North Macedonia.
items.summary: From 1 January 2008, emigration accelerated because of visa-free Schengen entry following the 2007 EU visa facilitation and readmission agreements.
items.extraction_note: Event before the run's time window, kept only because it explains the origin of current emigration; no exception is logged in limits_log.csv, so the analyst must confirm or exclude.

items.stated_text: According to Bulgarian authorities, over 90 000 Macedonians have obtained Bulgarian passports since 2002.
items.summary: According to Bulgarian authorities, over 90,000 Macedonians have obtained Bulgarian passports since 2002.
items.extraction_note: Figure reported by Bulgarian authorities and cited by the ETF. The introduction (page 8) gives a figure approaching 100 000 from a different Bulgarian source; not extracted.

items.stated_text: Macedonian emigrants are more often young, while their skills composition is mixed.
items.summary: Macedonian emigrants are more often young and have a mixed skills composition.

items.stated_text: Higher-educated emigrants predominantly live in overseas countries such as the US, Canada and Australia, while low- to medium-skilled emigrants mainly reside in Western European countries, which host the bulk of North Macedonia’s emigrants.
items.summary: Higher-educated emigrants mostly live overseas, while low- to medium-skilled emigrants mainly live in Western Europe, which hosts most emigrants.

items.stated_text: In general, emigration has been skewed towards people with a low level of education and, to a smaller but still substantial extent, people with a medium level of general education. This largely invalidates the brain-drain hypothesis, although particular occupations – most notably doctors, nurses and midwives – have exhibited intense emigration.
items.summary: Emigration is skewed towards low and medium education, largely invalidating the brain-drain hypothesis, though doctors, nurses and midwives emigrate intensely.

items.stated_text: The largest stock of Macedonian emigrants resides in Turkey, followed by Germany and other old Member States of the EU. Migration stock within the Western Balkans is mainly composed of emigrants to Serbia, but there has also been an emerging trend of emigration to some new Member States of the EU (e.g. Croatia and Slovenia), which likely involves circular migration.
items.summary: Most emigrants live in Turkey, then Germany and older EU Member States; emigration to Croatia and Slovenia is emerging, likely circular.
items.extraction_note: 'likely' hedges the circular migration claim.

items.stated_text: Over the years, Germany has showed persistent demand for medium- to high-skilled emigrants and enthusiasm for their eventual naturalisation.
items.summary: Germany has shown persistent demand for medium- to high-skilled emigrants and enthusiasm for their eventual naturalisation.

items.stated_text: Germany’s newly adopted Skilled Labour Immigration Act provides an opportunity for both North Macedonia and Germany to benefit by balancing Germany’s growing skills needs with North Macedonia’s desire to improve human capital and minimise the effects of its erosion in the domestic labour market.
items.summary: Germany's new Skilled Labour Immigration Act offers both countries an opportunity to balance German skills needs with Macedonian human capital goals.

items.stated_text: Pull factors for Macedonians include decent jobs, higher wages and better standards of living at destination. Push factors are multiple and more complex, ranging from the society’s widespread politicisation to dissatisfaction with the education system, healthcare and weak governance. The initial triggers, however, are low wages, long job queues, the wage premium in the public sector, and insecure jobs in the private sector.
items.summary: Emigration is pulled by better jobs, wages and living standards abroad and pushed by politicisation, services, weak governance, low wages and insecure jobs.

items.stated_text: Over time, earning a better income has outpaced family reunification as a reason to emigrate.
items.summary: Earning a better income has overtaken family reunification as a reason to emigrate.

items.stated_text: In addition to emigration, both the inflow of foreign direct investment (FDI) since 2007 and the government’s active labour market policies had sharply reduced unemployment.
items.summary: Emigration, foreign direct investment since 2007 and active labour market policies had sharply reduced unemployment before the pandemic.

items.stated_text: At the same time, however, emigration and FDI have predominantly sourced medium-level skills in the labour market.
items.summary: Emigration and foreign direct investment have mainly drawn on medium-level skills in the labour market.

items.stated_text: Vocational education and training (VET) and the development of the dual education system, which receives support from German-owned companies in North Macedonia, work to bridge the gap between the departing medium-skilled labour force and the domestic labour market’s growing demands.
items.summary: VET and the dual education system, supported by German-owned companies, help bridge the gap left by departing medium-skilled workers.
items.intervention_as_stated: Vocational education and training (VET) and the dual education system
items.extraction_note: Describes an existing system and what it does; could also be read as a finding. Included under Chapter 2 because the source ties it to emigration of medium-skilled workers.

items.stated_text: Skills obtained in the domestic education system play a mixed role in emigration. Some emigrants find their skills to be sufficient and relevant at destination, while others acquire additional skills either prior to departure or at destination.
items.summary: Domestic education plays a mixed role: some emigrants find their skills sufficient abroad, others acquire more skills before or after leaving.

items.stated_text: In addition, reforms in the education system have promoted the acquisition of IT and language skills that may ultimately foster more emigration.
items.summary: Education reforms promoting IT and language skills may ultimately foster more emigration.
items.extraction_note: 'may' hedges the claim. The reference to IT skills is incidental for the technology theme, so no theme tag.

items.stated_text: Among Macedonian emigrants, the propensity to return remains low. This implies that any skills learnt abroad are unlikely to contribute to the aims of domestic development.
items.summary: Emigrants rarely return, so skills learnt abroad are unlikely to contribute to domestic development.

items.stated_text: Although government policies to re-import skills have been weak in recent decades, the economic context has not been conducive either. Nor has the country been able to compete well against the targeted skills attraction strategies devised by more advanced countries with accelerated ageing and skills replacement needs.
items.summary: Weak government skills re-import policies, an unfavourable economic context and competition from advanced countries' skills attraction strategies limit returns.

items.stated_text: However, several notions that are prominent in public debates, such as mass exodus and brain drain, should be approached with caution, because they may contain elements of fallacy that are further complicated by any new realities that may arise from the Covid-19 pandemic in this regard.
items.summary: Notions such as mass exodus and brain drain should be approached with caution because they may contain elements of fallacy.
items.extraction_note: 'may contain' hedges the claim.

items.stated_text: We also note that emigration, particularly the recent waves, is likely to be more permanent in character, because entire families have departed and no significant return migration has occurred even during the pandemic.
items.summary: Recent emigration is likely more permanent, as whole families have left and no significant return occurred even during the pandemic.
items.extraction_note: 'is likely to be' hedges the claim.

items.stated_text: We find that wage differentials and wage-to-consumption-basket ratios between destination countries and home are very wide and appear both in low- to medium-skill jobs, such as those in manufacturing, and in high-skill specialised jobs.
items.summary: Wage gaps and wage-to-consumption-basket ratios between destination countries and home are very wide in both low- and high-skill jobs.

items.stated_text: However, as emigrants are widely distributed along the skills scale, there is no convincing evidence that recent spikes in wage-related migrations have disproportionally depleted Macedonian high-skill professionals, even though they remain vocal in the public debate.
items.summary: There is no convincing evidence that recent wage-related migration has disproportionately depleted high-skill professionals.

items.stated_text: Germany mainly attracts medium-skilled Macedonian workers, who are increasingly likely to emigrate with their entire family (spouse and children).
items.summary: Germany mainly attracts medium-skilled Macedonian workers, who increasingly emigrate with their whole family.

items.stated_text: In view of Germany’s new Skilled Labour Immigration Act, Western Balkan countries including North Macedonia may attempt to negotiate a comprehensive arrangement with Germany that would benefit both parties by balancing Germany’s growing high-skill needs with the Macedonian desire to improve human capital and minimise the effect of its erosion on the domestic labour market.
items.summary: North Macedonia, with other Western Balkan countries, may try to negotiate a mutually beneficial comprehensive migration arrangement with Germany.

items.stated_text: The key German consultant to the Government of North Macedonia, who is a direct support provided by German Chancellor Angela Merkel and may potentially garner the backing of the German– Macedonian Business Association, could create fertile ground for progress on the issue.
items.summary: A key German consultant to the government, supported by Chancellor Merkel, could create fertile ground for progress on an arrangement.
items.extraction_note: 'may potentially' and 'could' hedge the claim.

items.stated_text: The new EU Pact on Migration and Asylum, which was announced by the European Commission on 23 September 2020, might present an opportunity in this regard, as it includes two proposals for the management of labour migration at the EU level (European Commission, 2020).
items.summary: The EU Pact on Migration and Asylum, announced on 23 September 2020, might offer an opportunity through two labour migration proposals.
items.extraction_note: 'might' hedges the claim. The event date is the announcement of the Pact. The following description of Talent Partnerships and the EU Talent Pool is background on EU proposals and was not extracted.

items.stated_text: Intense emigration aggravates labour market fragilities.
items.summary: Intense emigration aggravates labour market fragilities.

items.stated_text: In early 2020 the unemployment rate was still at about 16%, but at the same time skills shortages were the most important problem in business climate surveys after having been virtually non-existent in the 2000s.
items.summary: In early 2020 unemployment was about 16 percent, while skills shortages had become the top problem in business climate surveys.
items.extraction_note: Included because the source presents skills shortages as a result of emigration and FDI (preceding sentence).

items.stated_text: FDI and emigration compete for the same pool of labour, but emigration frequently wins because of wage differentials and robust employment conditions abroad.
items.summary: FDI and emigration compete for the same workers, and emigration often wins because of wage gaps and better conditions abroad.

items.stated_text: In the same vein, the development of the dual education system, which is heavily supported by German-owned companies in North Macedonia, should be nurtured to bridge the gap between the departing medium-skilled labour force and the increasing domestic demands that are being driven by reindustrialisation.
items.summary: The dual education system should be nurtured to bridge the gap left by departing medium-skilled workers.

items.stated_text: On the other hand, the effects of emigration on the domestic education system are at best limited: programmes have certainly been reconfigured to reflect global trends, but skills acquired abroad are rarely used fruitfully in North Macedonia, either because the propensity for return migration is very low or because inefficiencies in government policies (e.g. providing scholarships to study at the top 500 universities) deter high-skill returnees even when they are obliged to return.
items.summary: Skills acquired abroad are rarely used because return migration is very low and policy inefficiencies deter high-skill returnees.

items.stated_text: 1. North Macedonia needs a comprehensive strategy on economic migration. The existing National Diaspora Strategy can serve as a decent starting point, which may be expanded not only to cover what the diaspora can contribute to the country’s development trajectory, but also how to manage potential (post-pandemic) growth in the emigration of labour (low- to medium-skill) and human capital (medium- to high-skill), especially to countries that demonstrate an ongoing appetite for an array of qualified workers, like Germany.
items.summary: A comprehensive economic migration strategy is needed, possibly expanding the National Diaspora Strategy to manage emigration of labour and human capital.

items.stated_text: 2. North Macedonia needs a cross-institutional approach for handling economic migration. The country’s stakeholders need to find the most efficient approach to achieve cross-institutional coordination of all aspects of migration.
items.summary: North Macedonia needs a cross-institutional approach to economic migration, with efficient coordination of all aspects of migration.

location.section: 6. CONCLUSIONS AND POLICY IMPLICATIONS, Policy implications

items.extraction_note: Policy implication 2. Also summarised in the key messages (page 7), not extracted twice.

items.stated_text: This may involve a need to designate a body to provide coordination between various government institutions that are relevant for migration (e.g. the Ministry of Labour and Social Policy, the Ministry of Economy, the Ministry of Finance, the Employment Service Agency and the Migration Agency) and non-governmental economic organisations, such as chambers of commerce, employers’ organisations, trade unions, think tanks, etc. Alternatively, migration issues may be mainstreamed within existing inter-institutional and social dialogue mechanisms.
items.summary: A body could coordinate migration across ministries, agencies and economic organisations, or migration could be mainstreamed in existing dialogue mechanisms.

items.stated_text: 3. North Macedonia needs reliable and comprehensive data on migration produced domestically.
items.summary: North Macedonia needs reliable and comprehensive domestically produced data on migration.

items.stated_text: However, beyond the Census, the State Statistical Office needs to consider the option to devise an bi-annual module on migration to be attached either to the Labour Force Survey or the Survey on Income and Living Conditions, hence collecting more detailed data on the skills levels and occupations of emigrants abroad and returnees as well as remittances.
items.summary: The State Statistical Office should consider a twice-yearly migration module in the Labour Force Survey or SILC on emigrants, returnees and remittances.

items.stated_text: 4. The relationship with Germany should be nurtured. Given that Germany’s Skilled Labour Immigration Act is expected to increase economic emigration from North M acedonia to Germany, the government should seek positive externalit ies, like re-importing skills acquired in Germany.
items.summary: The relationship with Germany should be nurtured, and the government should seek benefits such as re-importing skills acquired there.

items.stated_text: 6. The government should ensure that all policies that affect particularly medium- to high-skilled workers are carefully thought out, especially in terms of their mutual consistency and their risk of exacerbating migration decisions.
items.summary: Policies affecting medium- to high-skilled workers should be consistent and avoid increasing the risk of emigration.

items.stated_text: For example, subsidising high wages and introducing progressive taxation are not mutually consistent, especially if applied to high-prospect sectors and/or occupations like IT professionals, and they may actually spur rapid emigration.
items.summary: Subsidising high wages while introducing progressive taxation is inconsistent and may spur rapid emigration, especially of IT professionals.

items.stated_text: However, when it comes to the risk of emigration, the system should focus on tailoring skills to match current demand in the labour market, especially skills where fast gains can be made.
items.summary: To address emigration risk, the education system should tailor skills to current labour market demand, especially where gains are fast.

This does not imply any importing of labour; quite the contrary, the policy to subsidise degrees abroad should be reinforced, with a strong return component and an obligation to transfer learnt skills to the domestic economy.
items.summary: Skills import should be redesigned: subsidised study abroad should be reinforced with a strong return component and duty to transfer skills.
